statement: Prove there are infinitely many quadruples of positive integers $(a,b,c,d)$ such that $ab+1$, $bc+16$, $cd+4$, $ad+9$ are all perfect squares.

In $\triangle ABC$, points $A_1, A_2 \in BC$; $B_1, B_2 \in CA$; $C_1, C_2 \in AB$ form a convex hexagon $A_1A_2B_1B_2C_1C_2$ with $B, A_1, A_2, C$ in that order on $BC$. Triangles $AB_2C_1$, $BA_1C_2$, $CA_2B_1$ are \textit{glueable} if they can be assembled as the three corner triangles of some triangle $PQR$. Prove they are glueable iff the centroids of $\triangle A_1B_1C_1$ and $\triangle A_2B_2C_2$ coincide.
Find all positive integers $n$ such that $3^n - 2^n - 1$ is a perfect square.

A positive integer $N$ with $2k$ digits is \textit{cearense} if: it has an even number of digits; its two $k$-digit chunks are coprime; and it divides its \textit{reverse} (formed by swapping the chunks). Find the two smallest cearense integers.
A permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ is \textit{magic} if each element $k$ has at least $\lfloor k/2 \rfloor$ elements smaller than it to its left. For each $n$, find the number of magic permutations.

On an $8 \times 8$ board with 64 kings (one per cell), Arnaldo and Bernaldo alternate. Each move: choose a king and move it right, up, or diagonally up-right. If a king lands on an occupied cell, both are removed. The player who removes the last two kings or leaves one king in the upper-right corner wins. Who wins with optimal play?
